claim: ATP-sensitive K+ channels (KATP) have three classes of nucleotide binding site (NBS).
source: The response of ATP-sensitive K+ channels (KATP) to cellular metabolism is coordinated by three classes of nucleotide binding site (NBS).
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a fundamental property of KATP channels.

claim: Binding to NBS2 of SUR1 is Mg2+-independent.
source: Binding to NBS2 was Mg2+-independent, but Mg2+ was required to trigger a conformational change in SUR1.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing TNP-nucleotide binding in the absence of Mg2+.

claim: Mg2+ is required to trigger a conformational change in SUR1.
source: Binding to NBS2 was Mg2+-independent, but Mg2+ was required to trigger a conformational change in SUR1.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by nucleotide dissociation rate experiments showing Mg2+-dependent slowing of off-rates.

claim: The K1384A mutation in NBS2 increases the EC50 for trinitrophenyl-ADP binding to NBS2 in the presence of Mg2+.
source: Mutation of a lysine (K1384A) in NBS2 that coordinates bound nucleotides increased the EC50 for trinitrophenyl-ADP binding to NBS2, but only in the presence of Mg2+, indicating that this mutation disrupts the ligand-induced conformational change.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by binding experiments comparing K1384A to wild-type.

claim: The K1384A mutation disrupts the ligand-induced conformational change in SUR1.
source: Mutation of a lysine (K1384A) in NBS2 that coordinates bound nucleotides increased the EC50 for trinitrophenyl-ADP binding to NBS2, but only in the presence of Mg2+, indicating that this mutation disrupts the ligand-induced conformational change.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation in the abstract, supported by the observation that K1384A only affects binding in the presence of Mg2+.

claim: Each nucleotide binding event to NBS2 of SUR1 is independent.
source: Comparison of nucleotide-binding with ionic currents suggests a model in which each nucleotide binding event to NBS2 of SUR1 is independent and promotes KATP activation by the same amount.
evidence: Stated in the abstract based on comparison of binding and current data fit to MWC model.

claim: Each nucleotide binding event to NBS2 of SUR1 promotes KATP activation by the same amount.
source: Comparison of nucleotide-binding with ionic currents suggests a model in which each nucleotide binding event to NBS2 of SUR1 is independent and promotes KATP activation by the same amount.
evidence: Stated in the abstract based on MWC model fitting to combined binding and current data.

claim: KATP channel closure initiates the electrical response of pancreatic β-cells to metabolic changes induced by increased extracellular glucose.
source: ATP-sensitive K+ channel (KATP) closure initiates the electrical response of pancreatic β-cells to metabolic changes induced by increased extracellular glucose (Ashcroft and Rorsman, 2013; Quan et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: KATP's metabolic sensitivity is accomplished through the coordinated activity of three classes of intracellular adenine nucleotide binding site, one inhibitory and two stimulatory.
source: KATP's metabolic sensitivity is accomplished through the coordinated activity of three classes of intracellular adenine nucleotide binding site (NBS), one inhibitory and two stimulatory.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as established knowledge about KATP function.

claim: KATP is formed by four inward-rectifier K+ channel subunits (Kir6.2 in β-cells), each associated with a modulatory sulfonylurea receptor (SUR1 in β-cells).
source: KATP is formed by four inward-rectifier K+ channel subunits (Kir6.2 in β-cells), each associated with a modulatory sulfonylurea receptor (SUR1 in β-cells, Figure 1a) (Inagaki et al., 1995; Sakura et al., 1995; Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1997).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The inhibitory NBS of KATP is located on Kir6.2.
source: The inhibitory NBS of KATP is located on Kir6.2 and clearly resolved in several of the cryo-EM structures (Lee et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017a; Puljung, 2018; Wu et al., 2018; Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: SUR1 has two cytoplasmic nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), which associate to form two NBSs at the dimer interface.
source: Like other ATP-binding cassette (ABC) proteins, SUR1 has two cytoplasmic nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), which associate to form two NBSs at the dimer interface (Figure 1a,c) (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with reference to structural data and Figure 1.

claim: NBS2 is formed primarily by the nucleotide-binding WalkerA and WalkerB motifs of NBD2 and the ABC signature sequence of NBD1.
source: NBS2, formed primarily by the nucleotide-binding WalkerA and WalkerB motifs of NBD2 and the ABC signature sequence of NBD1, is a consensus binding site, based on conservation of key catalytic residues with other ABC family members, and is competent to hydrolyze nucleotides (de Wet et al., 2007; Matsuo et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: NBS2 is competent to hydrolyze nucleotides.
source: NBS2, formed primarily by the nucleotide-binding WalkerA and WalkerB motifs of NBD2 and the ABC signature sequence of NBD1, is a consensus binding site, based on conservation of key catalytic residues with other ABC family members, and is competent to hydrolyze nucleotides (de Wet et al., 2007; Matsuo et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In NBS1, the catalytic WalkerB glutamate is replaced with an aspartate (D854), rendering this site 'degenerate' and incapable of nucleotide hydrolysis.
source: In NBS1, formed by the Walker motifs of NBD1 and the signature sequence of NBD2, the catalytic WalkerB glutamate is replaced with an aspartate (D854), rendering this site 'degenerate,' that is, incapable of nucleotide hydrolysis.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a structural feature with functional consequence.

claim: NBS1 binds nucleotides in the absence of Mg2+.
source: NBS1 binds nucleotides in the absence of Mg2+, whereas it is thought that Mg2+ is required for binding to NBS2 (Matsuo et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: The NBSs of SUR1 mediate KATP activation by Mg-nucleotides.
source: The NBSs of SUR1 mediate KATP activation by Mg-nucleotides (Tucker et al., 1997; Nichols et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SUR1 confers inhibition by antidiabetic sulfonylureas (SUs) and activation by KATP-specific K+ channel openers (KCOs).
source: SUR1 also confers inhibition by antidiabetic sulfonylureas (SUs) and activation by KATP-specific K+ channel openers (KCOs) (Tucker et al., 1997; Nichols et al., 1996; Gribble et al., 1997a; Gribble et al., 1997b).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MgTNP-ADP bound to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 with an EC50 of approximately 4.8 µM.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1f legend and shown in the concentration-response curve.

claim: MgTNP-ATP bound to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 with an EC50 of approximately 29.3 µM.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1f legend and shown in the concentration-response curve.

claim: TNP-ADP bound to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 in the absence of Mg2+ with an EC50 of approximately 6.1 µM.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1g legend and shown in the concentration-response curve.

claim: TNP-ATP bound to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 in the absence of Mg2+ with an EC50 of approximately 8.5 µM.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1g legend and shown in the concentration-response curve.

claim: MgTNP-ADP was able to activate KATP formed by wild-type SUR1 with mutated Kir6.2-G334D in inside-out patches.
source: MgTNP-ADP was able to activate KATP formed by wild-type SUR1 with a mutated Kir6.2 (Kir6.2-G334D) in inside-out patches (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c,d; Table 1).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to supplementary figure showing current traces and concentration-response.

claim: G334D disrupts inhibitory nucleotide binding to Kir6.2, allowing activation to be measured in isolation.
source: G334D disrupts inhibitory nucleotide binding to Kir6.2, allowing activation to be measured in isolation (Drain et al., 1998; Proks et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the text with supporting citations.

claim: TNP-ADP dissociated very rapidly from SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 in the absence of Mg2+.
source: In the absence of Mg2+, TNP-ADP dissociated very rapidly from SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 (Figure 2a,e; Table 3).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 2 showing dissociation time courses.

claim: Dissociation of TNP-ADP from SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 was greatly slowed by the presence of Mg2+.
source: Dissociation of TNP-ADP was greatly slowed by the presence of Mg2+ (p=0.001).
evidence: Stated in the text with statistical significance value.

claim: In the presence of tolbutamide, the dissociation rates for MgTNP-ADP and MgTNP-ATP were not significantly different from those measured for nucleotides in the absence of both tolbutamide and Mg2+.
source: In the presence of tolbutamide, the dissociation rates for MgTNP-ADP and MgTNP-ATP were not significantly different from those measured for nucleotides in the absence of both tolbutamide and Mg2+ (Figure 2e, Table 3; p=0.1, for TNP-ADP, p=1 for TNP-ATP).
evidence: Stated in the text with statistical values and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The slower off rate for TNP-ADP and TNP-ATP in the presence of Mg2+ results from NBD dimerization, not a direct stabilization of nucleotide binding by Mg2+.
source: This argues that the slower off rate for TNP-ADP and TNP-ATP in the presence of Mg2+ must result from NBD dimerization, not a direct stabilization of nucleotide binding by Mg2+.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation based on the tolbutamide experiment results.

claim: Diazoxide greatly reduced the dissociation rates for both MgTNP-ADP and MgTNP-ATP.
source: The time course of nucleotide dissociation in the presence of diazoxide did not closely follow a single exponential decay, but the drug greatly reduced the dissociation rates for both MgTNP-ADP and MgTNP-ATP (Figure 2c,d,e; Table 3).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 2 showing dissociation time courses.

claim: KCOs function by stabilizing the activated (NBD-dimerized) conformation of SUR1.
source: This suggests that KCOs function by stabilizing the activated (NBD-dimerized) conformation of SUR1.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation based on the diazoxide experiment results.

claim: The K2A mutation had no effect on the intrinsic nucleotide affinity in the absence of Mg2+.
source: In the absence of Mg2+, we observed no significant difference in steady-state TNP-ATP and TNP-ADP binding to SUR1-Y1353*,K2A/Kir6.2 compared to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 (Figure 3b,c; Table 2), suggesting the K2A mutation has no effect on the intrinsic nucleotide affinity in the absence of Mg2+.
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 3 showing concentration-response curves.

claim: The K2A mutation disrupted MgTNP-ADP binding, increasing the EC50 from 4.8 μM to 18.6 μM.
source: However the K2A mutation disrupted MgTNP-ADP binding (EC50 = 18.6 μM for K2A vs. 4.8 μM for SUR1-Y1353*, p=0.04; Figure 3e, Table 2).
evidence: Stated in the text with statistical significance and reference to Figure 3.

claim: The K2A mutation increased the off-rate for MgTNP-ADP compared to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 channels.
source: The K2A mutation increased the off-rate for MgTNP-ADP compared to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 channels (Table 3; p=0.04).
evidence: Stated in the text with statistical significance.

claim: The K2A mutation destabilized NBD dimerization induced by MgTNP-ADP.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the K2A mutation destabilized NBD dimerization induced by MgTNP-ADP.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation based on the combined binding and dissociation data for K2A mutant.

claim: SUR1-Y1353* fails to support nucleotide activation of KATP channels.
source: This suggests that SUR-Y1353* fails to support nucleotide activation.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on electrophysiology experiments showing no activation by MgADP.

claim: SUR1-T1397* supported activation of Kir6.2-G334D by both MgADP and MgTNP-ADP.
source: More importantly, SUR1-T1397* supported activation of Kir6.2-G334D by both MgADP (Figure 4d, Table 1) and MgTNP-ADP (Figure 5a,b; Table 1).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to figures showing current activation.

claim: The EC50 for channel activation by MgTNP-ADP was 7.3 μM ± 1.2 μM for SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2-G334D.
source: The EC50 for channel activation by MgTNP-ADP (determined from Hill fits) was 7.3 μM ± 1.2 μM as compared to the EC50 of 10.8 μM ± 0.7 μM obtained for MgTNP-ADP binding to NBS2.
evidence: Stated in the text comparing activation and binding EC50 values.

claim: The EC50 for MgTNP-ADP binding to NBS2 of SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2 was 10.8 μM ± 0.7 μM.
source: The EC50 for channel activation by MgTNP-ADP (determined from Hill fits) was 7.3 μM ± 1.2 μM as compared to the EC50 of 10.8 μM ± 0.7 μM obtained for MgTNP-ADP binding to NBS2.
evidence: Stated in the text comparing activation and binding EC50 values.

claim: The best fits to the combined binding and activation data were obtained with an extended Monod-Wyman-Changeux model.
source: With these assumptions, the best fits to the data were obtained with an extended Monod-Wyman-Changeux model (Figure 5b; R2 = 0.98, RSS = 0.15) (Monod et al., 1965).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 5 showing the model fit.

claim: In the MWC model, binding of MgTNP-ADP to each NBS2 of SUR1 is independent and favors pore opening by the same amount.
source: In this model, binding of MgTNP-ADP to each NBS2 of SUR1 is independent and favors pore opening by the same amount.
evidence: Stated as a description of the MWC model used to fit the data.

claim: Nucleotides can bind NBS2 in the absence of Mg2+, but Mg2+ is required to support the conformational change that promotes channel activation.
source: If nucleotides can bind NBS2 in the absence of Mg2+, why is KATP only activated in the presence of Mg2+? The simplest explanation is that binding to NBS2 is Mg2+-independent, but Mg2+ is required to support the conformational change that promotes channel activation.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The conformational change in SUR1 required for channel activation involves NBD dimerization.
source: Presumably, this conformational change involves NBD dimerization, as observed in the cryo-EM structures of KATP (Lee et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to structural studies.

claim: Nucleotide dissociation requires opening of the NBD dimer.
source: Because nucleotide dissociation would require opening of the NBD dimer, dimerization is expected to slow the nucleotide off rate.
evidence: Stated as a logical inference based on the structural requirement for nucleotide release.

claim: Inhibitory SUs prevent NBD dimerization.
source: Inhibitory SUs prevent NBD dimerization.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as part of the activation model, supported by tolbutamide experiments.

claim: KCOs stabilize NBD dimerization, prolonging nucleotide occupancy at NBS2 and channel activation.
source: KCOs have the opposite effect. They stabilize NBD dimerization, prolonging nucleotide occupancy at NBS2 and channel activation.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as part of the activation model, supported by diazoxide experiments.

claim: The affinities measured for TNP-ADP and TNP-ATP binding are higher than those previously estimated for ATP and ADP from photoaffinity labeling studies on SUR1 in the absence of Kir6.2 or from ATPase assays performed on isolated NBD2 fusion proteins.
source: The affinities we measured for TNP-ADP and TNP-ATP binding are higher than those previously estimated for ATP and ADP from photoaffinity labeling studies on SUR1 in the absence of Kir6.2 or from ATPase assays preformed on isolated NBD2 fusion proteins (de Wet et al., 2007; Matsuo et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion comparing current results to previous studies.

claim: The EC50 values obtained from MgTNP-ATP and MgTNP-ADP binding to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 were in reasonably good agreement with those measured for MgATP and MgADP activation of SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D currents.
source: Nevertheless, the EC50 values obtained from MgTNP-ATP and MgTNP-ADP binding to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 were in reasonably good agreement with those measured for MgATP and MgADP activation of SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D currents (Proks et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion comparing binding and activation data.

claim: MgADP can activate channels to an equal or greater extent than MgATP.
source: MgADP can activate channels to an equal or greater extent than MgATP (Proks et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The act of ATP hydrolysis per se is not required for channel activation.
source: Therefore, it is clear that the act of ATP hydrolysis per se is not required for channel activation, even though NBS2 is competent to hydrolyze ATP (de Wet et al., 2007; Matsuo et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on MgADP activation data.

claim: There is no evidence that an irreversible step like ATP hydrolysis occurs during the gating cycle of the KATP channel in the presence of MgATP.
source: However, there is no evidence that an irreversible step like ATP hydrolysis occurs during the gating cycle of the KATP channel in the presence of MgATP, as is the case for the closely related ABC protein CFTR (Choi et al., 2008; Csanády et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with citations to related work on CFTR.

claim: ATP hydrolysis did not occur over the course of the experiments, as the off-rate for MgTNP-ATP was faster than that of MgTNP-ADP.
source: Our data suggest that ATP hydrolysis did not occur over the course of our experiments, as the off-rate for MgTNP-ATP was faster than that of MgTNP-ADP (t0.5 = 10.5 s vs 14.7 s).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the dissociation rate data.

claim: If MgTNP-ATP were hydrolysed to MgTNP-ADP before being released, the dissociation rates should have been similar.
source: If MgTNP-ATP were hydrolysed to MgTNP-ADP before being released (as is thought to be true of many ABC family members, including CFTR) the dissociation rates should have been similar.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a logical expectation if hydrolysis occurred.

claim: ANAP was introduced at position Y1353 of NBS2 using a transfectable amber codon suppression system.
source: ANAP was introduced at position Y1353 (Y1353*, Figure 1c) of NBS2 using a transfectable amber codon suppression system (Chatterjee et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the experimental method.

claim: In the nucleotide-bound structures of KATP, the aromatic ring of Y1353 forms a π-stacking interaction with the adenine ring of ADP.
source: In the nucleotide-bound structures of KATP, the aromatic ring of Y1353 forms a π-stacking interaction with the adenine ring of ADP (Figure 1c) (Lee et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to structural data and Figure 1c.

claim: FRET between SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 and bound TNP-ADP produced a concentration-dependent decrease (quenching) of the donor ANAP peak at 470 nm and a concomitant increase in the TNP-ADP fluorescence at ~565 nm.
source: FRET between SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 and bound TNP-ADP produced a concentration-dependent decrease (quenching) of the donor ANAP peak at 470 nm and a concomitant increase in the TNP-ADP fluorescence at ~565 nm (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to Figure 1 showing spectral data.

claim: No change in fluorescence was observed when saturating concentrations of MgATP or MgADP were applied to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 channels.
source: No change in fluorescence was observed when saturating concentrations of MgATP or MgADP were applied to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2f), indicating that quenching of the ANAP signal results from FRET and not an allosteric change in the environment surrounding Y1353* caused by nucleotide binding.
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: MgTNP-ADP bound with ~7 fold lower EC50 than MgTNP-ATP to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2.
source: MgTNP-ADP bound with ~7 fold lower EC50 than MgTNP-ATP (Table 2), consistent with the lower EC50 for activation of SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D channels by MgADP vs. MgATP (7.7 μM vs. 112 μM) (Proks et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Results comparing binding affinities.

claim: The FRET observed was primarily the result of quenching by TNP-ATP/ADP bound at NBS2.
source: Despite the relatively close proximity of NBS1 to Y1353* (39 Å to TNP-ATP aligned at NBS1, Figure 1c), the FRET we observed was primarily the result of quenching by TNP-ATP/ADP bound at NBS2.
evidence: Stated in the Results as an interpretation based on distance calculations.

claim: The EC50 for MgTNP-ADP binding to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2-G334D was very similar to that measured with SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2.
source: The EC50 was very similar to that measured with SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 (Table 2), suggesting that either the NBS on Kir6.2 was too distant for FRET with Y1353*, or that appreciable binding to Kir6.2 did not occur at concentrations at which NBS2 was unoccupied.
evidence: Stated in the Results comparing binding to different Kir6.2 variants.

claim: Mg2+ caused a rightward shift in the concentration dependence of nucleotide binding to SUR1-Y1353*,K2A/Kir6.2.
source: Similar to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 channels, Mg2+ caused a rightward shift in the concentration dependence of nucleotide binding to SUR1-Y1353*,K2A/Kir6.2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The apparent affinity for ATP inhibition of SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2 was lower than for wild-type KATP (IC50 was 53.9 μM vs. 11.2 μM).
source: Interestingly, the apparent affinity for ATP inhibition of SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2 was lower than for wild-type KATP (IC50 was 53.9 μM vs. 11.2 μM, respectively; Table 5).
evidence: Stated in the Results comparing ATP inhibition between constructs.

claim: Mg2+ decreased the intrinsic on-rate for nucleotide binding (kon) to NBS2.
source: As we observed such a shift for Mg-TNP-ATP, we conclude that in addition to stabilizing the NBDs in a dimerized state when nucleotides are present, Mg2+ must also decrease the intrinsic on-rate for nucleotide binding (kon).
evidence: Stated in the Results as a conclusion based on the rightward shift in EC50 for MgTNP-ATP.

claim: The nucleotide dissociation rates measured in the presence of Mg2+ are slower than the deactivation rates observed for SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D currents following nucleotide washout.
source: The nucleotide dissociation rates measured in the presence of Mg2+ are slower than the deactivation rates observed for SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D currents following nucleotide washout (Proks et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Results comparing dissociation rates to deactivation rates from literature.

claim: Current decay reflects a conformational change in the channel and not the rate of nucleotide dissociation.
source: However, it should be noted that current decay reflects a conformational change in the channel and not the rate of nucleotide dissociation, and may be affected by the presence of four SUR1 monomers per channel.
evidence: Stated in the Results as an explanation for the difference between dissociation and deactivation rates.

claim: The WalkerA lysine coordinates the β- and γ-phosphates of bound nucleotides in other ABC proteins and in the Mg-nucleotide-bound structure of KATP.
source: In other ABC proteins, and in the Mg-nucleotide-bound structure of KATP, the WalkerA lysine coordinates the β- and γ-phosphates of bound nucleotides (Figure 3a).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to Figure 3a showing the structural interaction.

claim: Mutation of the WalkerA lysine in NBS2 to alanine (K1384A, K2A) reduced the maximal activation of SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D currents by MgATP.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies showed that mutation of the WalkerA lysine in NBS2 to alanine (K1384A, K2A) reduced the maximal activation of SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D currents by MgATP and shifted the concentration dependence of MgADP activation >20 fold to higher concentrations, such that the maximal response could not be determined (Proks et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Results citing previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: The K1384A mutation shifted the concentration dependence of MgADP activation >20 fold to higher concentrations.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies showed that mutation of the WalkerA lysine in NBS2 to alanine (K1384A, K2A) reduced the maximal activation of SUR1/Kir6.2-G334D currents by MgATP and shifted the concentration dependence of MgADP activation >20 fold to higher concentrations, such that the maximal response could not be determined (Proks et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Results citing previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: Channels containing SUR1 subunits truncated at residue 1330 at the start of NBD2 traffic to the plasma membrane but are not activated by MgADP.
source: KATP channels with SUR1 truncated at residue 1330 at the start of NBD2, traffic to the plasma membrane but are not activated by MgADP (Sakura et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated in the Results with supporting citation.

claim: Truncated SUR1-Y1353stop/Kir6.2 formed functional channels that were not activated by MgADP.
source: Truncated SUR1-Y1353stop/Kir6.2 (expressed without pANAP) formed functional channels that were not activated by MgADP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure showing current data.

claim: 100 μM MgADP increased full-length 3xFLAG_SUR1/Kir6.2 currents 3.6-fold over the current in nucleotide-free control solutions.
source: 100 μM MgADP increased full-length 3xFLAG_SUR1/Kir6.2 currents 3.6-fold over the current in nucleotide-free control solutions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, Table 4).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure and table.

claim: 100 μM MgADP inhibited current from truncated SUR1-Y1353stop by 59%.
source: In contrast, 100 μM MgADP inhibited current from truncated SUR1-Y1353stop by 59% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, Table 4).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure and table.

claim: SUR1-Y1353* fails to support nucleotide activation based on electrophysiology experiments.
source: To confirm this, we also looked at currents in patches excised from cells expressing SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2-G334D (co-expressed with pANAP and pERF1-E55D). Wild-type SUR1 paired with Kir6.2-G334D produced channels that were activated by MgADP and inhibited by tolbutamide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c). When measured under the same conditions, SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 was inhibited by tolbutamide, but we observed no activation by MgADP.
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure showing current traces.

claim: SUR1-T1397stop strongly increased the surface expression of HA-Kir6.2 in the presence of ANAP.
source: We focused on SUR1-T1397stop, as this construct strongly increased the surface expression of HA-Kir6.2 in the presence of ANAP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a; p=0.005).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure and statistical significance.

claim: In the absence of ANAP, SUR1-T1397stop decreased the surface expression of HA-Kir6.2 compared to no-SUR1 controls.
source: Further, in the absence of ANAP, this construct decreased the surface expression of HA-Kir6.2 (p=0.009) compared to no-SUR1 controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), suggesting that channels with SUR truncated at this position may be selectively retained within the cell.
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure and statistical significance.

claim: Western blots confirmed that >95% of SUR1-T1397* was full length when expressed in the presence of ANAP and pANAP/peRF1-E55D.
source: Western blots of total protein from cells expressing SUR1-T1397stop in the presence of ANAP and pANAP/peRF1-E55D confirmed that >95% of SUR1-T1397* was full length (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure showing western blot.

claim: The expected distance between T1397* and TNP-nucleotides bound to NBS2 is ~18.3 Å.
source: The expected distance between T1397* and TNP-nucleotides bound to NBS2 is ~18.3 Å (Figure 4a), close enough for >99% FRET efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to Figure 4a showing the structure.

claim: Binding of MgTNP-ADP and MgTNP-ATP to SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2 was qualitatively similar to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2.
source: Binding of MgTNP-ADP and MgTNP-ATP to SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2 (Figure 4b) was qualitatively similar to SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2 (Figure 1, Table 2), although there was no obvious difference in binding affinity between MgTNP-ADP and MgTNP-ATP for SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2.
evidence: Stated in the Results comparing binding data between constructs.

claim: Both TNP-ADP and TNP-ATP bound to SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2 in the absence of Mg2+.
source: Both TNP-ADP and TNP-ATP bound to SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2 in the absence of Mg2+ (Figure 4c; Table 2) as we observed for SUR1-Y1353*/Kir6.2.
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: In excised patches from cells expressing SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2, robust currents were measured that were inhibited by ATP.
source: In excised patches from cells expressing SUR1-T1397*/Kir6.2, we measured robust currents that were inhibited by ATP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Stated in the Results with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Mutations that directly disrupt the NBSs or their ability to transduce nucleotide occupancy to the pore result in diseases of insulin secretion.
source: Mutations that directly disrupt the NBSs or their ability to transduce nucleotide occupancy to the pore result in diseases of insulin secretion (Quan et al., 2011; Ashcroft et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of Kir6.2/SUR1 in the presence of glibenclamide suggests that SUs prevent NBD dimerization.
source: The cryo-EM structure of Kir6.2/SUR1 in the presence of glibenclamide suggests that SUs prevent NBD dimerization, and electrophysiological studies further demonstrate that SUs prevent Mg-nucleotide induced current activation (Martin et al., 2017a; Proks et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Results with supporting citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: Electrophysiological studies demonstrate that SUs prevent Mg-nucleotide induced current activation.
source: The cryo-EM structure of Kir6.2/SUR1 in the presence of glibenclamide suggests that SUs prevent NBD dimerization, and electrophysiological studies further demonstrate that SUs prevent Mg-nucleotide induced current activation (Martin et al., 2017a; Proks et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Results with supporting citations.

claim: It has been proposed that nucleotide binding at the NBDs of SUR2A stabilizes binding of the KCO pinacidil.
source: It has been proposed that nucleotide binding at the NBDs of SUR2A stabilizes binding of the KCO pinacidil (Gribble et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated in the Results with supporting citation.

claim: High concentrations of ATP have been shown to cause SUR1 to change conformation in the absence of Mg2+, under which conditions ATP hydrolysis is not expected.
source: Furthermore, high concentrations of ATP have been shown, in radioligand binding assays, to cause SUR1 to change conformation in the absence of Mg2+, under which conditions ATP hydrolysis is not expected (Ortiz et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: Mg2+-free ATP, at high concentrations, was recently demonstrated to activate KATP formed by SUR1-Q1179R paired with Kir6.2-G334D.
source: Mg2+-free ATP, at high concentrations, was also recently demonstrated to activate KATP formed by SUR1-Q1179R, a gain-of-function SUR1 mutation, paired with Kir6.2-G334D, as well as SUR constructs in which the WalkerB glutamate was mutated to glutamine (Sikimic et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: No Mg2+-free ATP activation was demonstrated when wild-type SUR1 was expressed with Kir6.2-G334D.
source: No Mg2+-free ATP activation was demonstrated when wild-type SUR1 was expressed with Kir6.2-G334D and we see no indication in our data that nucleotides caused SUR1 to change conformation in the absence of Mg2+ (Figure 2) (Sikimic et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 2 and citation.

claim: The observation that MgTNP-ATP dissociation was faster than MgTNP-ADP dissociation may reflect a lack of MgTNP-ATP hydrolysis during the course of the experiments.
source: The observation that MgTNP-ATP dissociation was faster than MgTNP-ADP dissociation may reflect a lack of MgTNP-ATP hydrolysis during the course of our experiments.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the dissociation rate data.

claim: The faster dissociation of MgTNP-ATP compared to MgTNP-ADP may indicate a destabilizing effect of inorganic phosphate on MgTNP-ADP binding to NBS2.
source: Alternatively, this may indicate a destabilizing effect of inorganic phosphate on MgTNP-ADP binding to NBS2 (which would not be present when binding MgTNP-ADP alone, but would be present as a product of MgTNP-ATP hydrolysis) on binding.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an alternative interpretation.

claim: The method developed in this study is readily adaptable to the study of other ABC proteins and ATP-gated channels like P2X receptors.
source: It has also not escaped our notice that our method is readily adaptable to the study of other ABC proteins, ATP-gated channels like P2X receptors (for which different subtypes demonstrate distinct selectivity for MgATP vs. ATP) and any protein for which there is a suitable fluorescent ligand (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a broader application of the method.
